what_its_for: Levonorgestrel is an emergency contraceptive, sometimes called the 'morning-after pill.' It helps prevent pregnancy after unprotected sex or if your regular birth control failed (like a broken condom or missed pill). It works best when taken as soon as possible after unprotected sex. It is NOT the same as the abortion pill and will NOT end an existing pregnancy.
how_to_take: Take this medication by mouth with or without food. If you vomit within 2 hours of taking the pill, call your doctor or pharmacist right away because you may need to take another dose. You can take it at any time of day. No special instructions are needed — just swallow the tablet whole with a glass of water.
dosing: The standard dose is ONE tablet (1.5 mg) taken as soon as possible after unprotected sex. It works best within 72 hours (3 days), but can still offer some protection up to 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected sex. The sooner you take it, the better it works. This is a one-time dose — you do not need to take it more than once per episode of unprotected sex.
missed_dose: There is no missed dose with this medication because it is a single one-time pill. However, time is very important — the sooner you take it after unprotected sex, the more effective it will be. Do not delay taking it while waiting for the 'right time.'
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking this medication if you are already pregnant, as it will not work and is not intended to end a pregnancy. Avoid using this as regular ongoing birth control — it is only for emergencies and is less effective than daily birth control methods. Avoid taking extra doses thinking it will work better. Certain medications like rifampin (an antibiotic), seizure medications (such as phenytoin, carbamazepine), and St. John's Wort herbal supplement may make levonorgestrel less effective — talk to your pharmacist if you take any of these.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get medical help if: you vomit within 2 hours of taking the pill; you have severe stomach or abdominal pain (this could be a sign of an ectopic pregnancy, which is a medical emergency); your period is more than 1 week late after taking this medication; you think you might be pregnant; you experience heavy or unusual bleeding; or you have questions about whether your current medications may affect how well this pill works.
when_it_works: Levonorgestrel works mainly by delaying or preventing ovulation (the release of an egg). It may also affect the lining of the uterus or the movement of sperm. It does NOT cause an abortion or harm an existing pregnancy. You should expect your next menstrual period within 3 weeks of taking it. Your period may come earlier, later, or be slightly different than usual — this is normal. If your period does not come within 3 weeks, take a pregnancy test.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use if you are already pregnant — it will not work and will not harm an existing pregnancy. Breastfeeding: A small amount of levonorgestrel may pass into breast milk. Consider pumping and discarding breast milk for 24 hours after taking it if you are concerned. Weight: Some studies suggest this medication may be less effective in people weighing more than 165–175 pounds (75–80 kg). If this applies to you, talk to your healthcare provider about a more effective emergency contraceptive option, such as the copper IUD or ulipristal acetate (ella). Age: This medication is safe for teenagers and adults. It is available over the counter without a prescription for people of all ages.
